title: Coping With the Loneliness of Leadership
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article argues that leadership is inherently lonely because leaders cannot share the emotional weight of hard decisions with anyone inside the organization. It lists the sources of that weight, including decisions that hurt team members, staff departures and disappointing people with ideas that cannot be executed. The author warns that bottling these feelings up leads to stress, burnout, self-loathing or indifference. The remedy is to build an outlet outside the organization, such as family, friends, mentors, coaches or therapists, who can act as a sounding board. The practical move is to arrange this deliberately and in advance, telling people what role you want them to play rather than waiting for a crisis.
points: Loneliness grows with seniority because decisions become more consequential and there is no peer inside the organization to confide in.
Unprocessed frustration is presented as a direct path to stress, burnout and indifference.
The outlet should come from outside the organization: family, friends, mentors, executive coaches or therapists.
Recruit your sounding boards before you need them and tell them what role you want them to play.
quotes: At times, leadership can be a tremendously lonely experience. The emotional fallout of making difficult decisions that negatively affect the lives of some team members, the feeling of rejection when team members leave for other opportunities, and the discomfort of disappointing passionate team members who offer ideas that can’t be executed in the moment, among many other leadership acts, all take their toll.

There’s no one within the organization to complain to, commiserate with, or offload the heavy burden of emotions connected to leadership. This makes for some tough sledding anytime a leader temporarily loses their footing and confidence or faces an extreme test.

Keeping the negative feelings and frustrations bottled up inside is a recipe for stress, unhappiness, and burnout. Without the ability to vent and seek catharsis, leaders can turn inward and engage in self-loathing or become indifferent.

Leaders need an outlet to explore their feelings and to validate the worth of their choices. Trusting and willing family members, friends, mentors, executive coaches, and therapists are worth their weight in gold when they are open to patiently listen to a leader explain what is going on with them.

Finding an outlet shouldn’t happen by chance. Asking those you trust to play this role on occasion is essential before the need arises. Letting others know the role you would like them to play gives them a choice and a heads up.

Learning to swallow your pride and leaning on those who are ready to lend a hand makes the loneliness of leadership more bearable. Leaders often act alone but always walk with those outside the organization who care most about them.
